title: Tiered latency‑favoring router with soft geo‑anchors and capacity throttles
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Goal: implement a tiered request router that (1) prefers low‑latency local regions when SLO budgets allow, (2) softly pins long‑lived sessions to geo anchors to preserve KV cache locality, and (3) enforces capacity‑aware throttles + circuit breakers to protect global SLOs.

Why now: recurring incidents during cross‑region spikes show that naive geo failover increases tail latency and TTL cache churn, causing regressed SLOs and elevated token costs. We need a middle path that keeps common traffic local while gracefully shedding or rehoming traffic under capacity stress.

Scope and non‑goals: this ticket implements the routing policy, simulator, canary rollout hooks, and dashboards. It does NOT replace the autoscaler; it will emit signals consumed by autoscaling and admission controllers. It also does not modify client SDKs (protocol remains same).

Core components:
- Latency tiers: define per‑region latency budget windows (p50/p95 targets) and compute a real‑time tier score.
- Soft geo anchors: session affinity that decays over time and allows controlled reassignment during capacity pressure to preserve KV cache hits.
- Capacity throttles and circuit breakers: token‑bucket backpressure per region + global circuit with multi‑level fallback (local -> neighboring region -> pooled remote).
- Probe & risk scoring: lightweight probes and success/failure rates drive hysteresis and eviction decisions; include probing budget to avoid probe storms.
- Simulator & chaos tests: offline traffic replay simulator + small‑scale chaos to validate failure modes before global rollout.

High‑level decision log:
- Chosen soft pin strategy (2026‑03‑03): preserve session KV locality by pinning on first successful completion, decay half‑life = 30m. Rationale: caching gives ~3x token savings on many workloads; hard pinning causes cold starts during evacuations.
- Chosen circuit breaker levels (2026‑03‑05): 3 levels — green (normal), amber (degraded, enable hedging to neighboring region), red (eviction + shed non‑essential traffic). Rationale: gives deterministic progression and simple operator mental model.
- Hedging policy (2026‑03‑06): baseline hedging only for requests with p95‑sensitive flags (internal routes or customers flagged in workspace). Hedging doubles egress but reduces tail latency for critical traffic.
- Load shedding order (2026‑03‑08): shed speculative/streaming/low‑importance routes first, then low‑tier customers, finally global best‑effort requests. Rationale: minimize revenue and customer‑visible degradation.

Tradeoffs discussed:
- Locality vs throughput: keeping traffic local preserves cache but risks overloading small regions. Mitigation: soft anchors + capacity throttles + quick global fallback.
- Cost vs latency (hedging): hedging reduces tail latency at cost of duplicate tokens. Mitigation: restrict hedging to flagged requests and implement hedged response deduplication accounting.
- Observability complexity: need per‑token and per‑session metrics (costly). Mitigation: sample token traces and rely on aggregate summaries for realtime decisions.

Rollout plan:
1) Implement router + simulator in staging (week 1–2).
2) Run historic traffic replays and synthetic spikes, tune thresholds (week 3).
3) Canary in eu‑west cluster for internal customers (10% traffic) + dashboards + alert thresholds (week 4).
4) Gradual ramp with automated rollback triggers tied to SLO regressions (week 5–6).

Observability & SLOs:
- New dashboards: per‑region request success, p50/p95 latency, KV cache hit ratio, throttle events, circuit state transitions.
- SLO guardrails: automated rollback if customer‑facing p95 increases > 10% vs baseline or error rate increases > 0.5% absolute for more than 3m.

acceptance_criteria: Router implements latency tier scoring and exposes per‑region tier metric
Soft geo anchors persist session affinity and decay with configurable half‑life
Circuit breaker transitions (green/amber/red) are logged and emit Prometheus metrics
Capacity throttle token buckets enforce per‑region admission under overload
Simulator reproduces 90% of observed incident traffic patterns and shows expected failover behavior
Canary rollout + dashboards + automated rollback rules in place

activity: 2026-03-02: Kickoff meeting with SRE, Platform, Runtime teams. Agreed on 30m anchor half‑life and 3 circuit levels.
2026-03-04: Design review with PM (Lydia Chen) — approved with followups: add per‑tenant soft caps and opt‑out flag for high‑security customers.

2026-03-06: Spike implemented: prototype token bucket throttle + simple amber hedging (GitHub PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/router/pull/138). Performance looks promising under synthetic load.
2026-03-08: Security review triaged. HSM/KMS not impacted; added note to ensure probe traffic is authenticated. (sec ticket: SEC-212)
2026-03-10: Simulator replay of 2026-02-11 incident shows 35% reduction in p95 tail when hedging enabled for critical routes. Need to tune hedging scope to reduce cost impact.
2026-03-12: Canary prep: dashboards wired, rollback playbook drafted. Target canary start date 2026-03-18.
